title: Veridian Telecom POC — end-to-end P95 SLA runbook and bottleneck analysis
content:
Executive summary:

This document captures the results and operational guidance from the Veridian Telecom POC focused on achieving a customer-facing P95 latency SLA for interactive query workloads. The POC evaluated realistic traffic shapes, candidate model variants, and deployment configurations to find an operational baseline that meets a 180ms P95 target for short interactive prompts (<=256 tokens) while keeping incremental per-token cost within the customer budget.

Goals and SLA:
- Primary SLA: P95 <= 180ms for end-to-end inference (API receive -> first-token delivered) on 256-token requests for the interactive route.
- Throughput target: sustain 120 RPS steady-state for the interactive route during peak (burst to 200 RPS acceptable for 2 min).
- Cost objective: incremental inference cost <= $0.45 per 1k generated tokens on average across peak traffic mix.
- Quality constraints: no model change that reduces top-level intent accuracy by more than 1.5% (baseline human-eval set).

Test matrix and hardware:
- Models tested:
  * Llama-2-70b-q4f16 (server-side quantized q4f16, baseline fidelity)
  * Mistral-instruct-13b-fp16 (smaller high-efficiency variant)
  * Llama-2-13b-q4_0 (aggressive quantized candidate)
- Runtime kernels: Redwood Dedicated runtime (A100-80GB optimized kernels), stock OpenVINO/ONNX path for CPU fallback not used.
- Hardware targets:
  * Dedicated A100-80GB (2x for primary baseline) — labelled RD-A100x2
  * AWS p4d.24xlarge (for cloud comparison)
  * On-prem test: single H100-80GB node provided by Veridian lab
- Network: intra-region (low-latency), simulated 5–12ms egress to customer edge to mimic real path.

Workloads and harness:
- Traffic shapes derived from Veridian production traces (anonymized): 70% short interactive queries (mean input tokens 40, mean generation 64), 20% medium completions (input 120, gen 128), 10% long jobs (input+gen > 512).
- Synthetic driver: k6 + custom runner that simulates connection churn and real client pacing; test harness records per-request end-to-end latency, model compute time, queue wait, and tail latencies per host.
- Warmup: 30k tokens static warmup per model variant, then rolling warmup traffic for 10 minutes prior to measurement window.
- Cache modes tested: KV cache enabled vs disabled; prefix caching enabled for repeated prompts (chat warm start).
- Batching: continuous batching with max batch_size {1,4,8,16} and latency budget knobs per route.

Key measurements (representative results from the canonical run on RD-A100x2):
- Baseline (Llama-2-70b-q4f16, batch 8, kv-cache on):
  * P50 latency: 58 ms
  * P90 latency: 120 ms
  * P95 latency: 172 ms (meets SLA)
  * P99 latency: 260 ms
  * Sustained throughput: 125 RPS (short-query mix)
  * GPU util: 68% avg, 93% busy windows
  * Cost: $0.39 per 1k gen tokens (inferred from infra amortization + runtime GPU time)
- Smaller model (Mistral-13b-fp16, batch 8):
  * P95: 95 ms
  * Sustained throughput: 210 RPS
  * Cost: $0.17 per 1k tokens
  * Quality delta: -2.1% on intent-eval (exceeds quality loss threshold for some query classes)
- Aggressive quant (Llama-2-13b-q4_0, batch 8):
  * P95: 82 ms
  * Throughput: 235 RPS
  * Cost: $0.14 per 1k tokens
  * Quality delta: -0.9% (acceptable for non-critical routes)

Bottleneck decomposition (canonical baseline):
- Service queueing (continuous batching) accounted for ~34% of P95; kernel execution time ~52%; serialization/network overhead ~14%.
- Burst behavior: short bursts (2 min @ 200 RPS) saturated single model host GPU memory allocation for 70b variant, causing transient queue growth and P99 spikes to ~480ms.
- KV cache effectiveness: for chat-style repeated prefixes, prefix caching reduced per-request compute tokens by ~18% and P95 by ~26% for affected sessions.

Operational findings and tradeoffs:
- Model choice: For strict fidelity-sensitive customer routes, Llama-2-70b-q4f16 on RD-A100x2 meets P95 & cost targets but needs careful burst provisioning. For most interactive query classes, Llama-2-13b-q4_0 gives better cost/latency with acceptable quality tradeoffs and is recommended for non-critical routes.
- Batching: raising max_batch to 16 improved tokens/sec by ~24% but pushed P95 beyond SLA on short interactive queries; recommended max_batch=8 with latency-aware decider.
- Autoscaling: reactive autoscaling alone was too slow for 2-minute bursts; pre-warmed burst pools (hot standby) or predictive scale-up based on traffic signals recommended.
- Fallback routing: configure a fallback policy that prefers smaller quantized model when hot-host queue length > threshold; this preserved availability and reduced observed P99 spikes.

Recommended production configuration (Veridian POC -> prod baseline):
- Route: interactive-short (<=256 tokens) -> primary: Llama-2-70b-q4f16 on RD-A100x2, fallback: Llama-2-13b-q4_0 (auto-failover).
- Runtime knobs: continuous_batch.max_batch=8, latency_budget_ms=120 (pre-first-token delivery), kv_cache=true for chat routes, streaming=false for short route to prioritize first-token latency.
- Pool sizing: 4 active A100-80GB hosts per region (handles 120 RPS with headroom); 2 warm standby hosts to handle 2-minute bursts.
- Canary and rollout: start with 10% of traffic on fallback policy, monitor p95 and top-level intent metrics for 48h before wider rollout.

Cost sensitivity analysis (short-route dominant workload):
- Switching baseline to Llama-2-13b-q4_0 reduces monthly inference cost ~39% (estimated) but requires targeted evals for session types that fail.
- Enabling prefix caching across chat sessions reduces cumulative tokens generated by ~12–18%, translating to ~10% monthly cost savings at scale.

Failure modes observed during POC:
- Memory fragmentation on A100 hosts under mixed batch sizes led to occasional OOMs in long-run stress tests; resolved by a runtime allocator patch and periodic host rotation.
- Network jitter to customer ingress caused small buffer delays — mitigated by increasing client-side retry windows rather than impacting server latency profiles.

Open items and next steps:
- Run a 72-hour soak with production traffic replay (SE-4127) to validate fragmentation fix under realistic churn.
- Add a lightweight on-host health signal to drive pre-warming scripts; integrate with Redwood Console runbooks for automated warm-standby spin-up.
- Complete targeted human-in-the-loop evals for the 13b quantized variant on 3 critical customer query classes (owner: Priya Raman).
- Finalize pricing estimate and contract language describing fallback routing behavior and cost-implications for Veridian.

Appendix — quick checklist for SE/ops to reproduce canonical run:
1) Provision RD-A100x2 image with runtime v0.24.1 and kernel patch KP-19 applied.
2) Load models to host with kv_cache enabled; pre-warm with the provided warmup script (bench/warmup/veridian_warmup.py).
3) Start driver using k6+runner with trace sample file traces/veridian-short-heavy.json; use 10 minute warmup then 30 minute measure window.
4) Capture telemetry: per-request latency, host GPU utilization, queue length, and per-token cost estimate exporter.
5) Validate canary routing by flipping 10% traffic to fallback and watch p95 and intent-eval for 48h.

Contact and owners:
- POC lead / owner: Morgan Patel (morgan@redwood.ai)
- SE engineering: Eli Wong, Jonas Becker
- Customer eng / integration: Priya Raman

Notes: this doc is a working runbook and should be treated as the authoritative operational notes for the Veridian POC. Any production rollout must follow the open items above and the standard Redwood deployment checklist.
